We also ran the alternative, one conversation per cell for the whole stream, and found that it measures something else. The transcript then carried everything a harness knew about a recurring task, so its re-exposure gains were in-context learning that every compaction and restart wiped, and prime-agent’s refinements lived in a session-local store that a restart discarded. Two harnesses also got worse as their context grew over the stream, which reflects compaction more than learning. A short run of the per-instance protocol then confirmed, from each harness’s files, that a session opens with only our observation and that the next session loads what was persisted.

Continual-ARC, a unify benchmark

Explore every run · Paper · Cite · Blog post · Leaderboard · Baselines · Training · Experiments · Runs · Data

ARC-AGI measures how efficiently a system picks up a new skill from a few examples, but it serves each task once. Continual-ARC serves a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions instead, in which the same tasks recur after dormant gaps with fresh instances while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance the learner may pay for one more demonstration or submit an answer, and it may try again after a wrong one. On an instance it solves, a wrong answer and a demonstration each cost one; an instance it does not solve costs the whole budget of sixteen, however it failed, and we charge the learner the share of that budget it used. [...] If you use Continual-ARC, its code, its runs or its website, please cite the paper:

`@article{lenton2026continualarc, title = {Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime}, author = {Lenton, Daniel and Arif, Yusha and Mahmood, Haris}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2611.14505}, year = {2026} }`

Apache-2.0. Re-ARC is MIT, ARC-AGI is Apache-2.0 and ARC-AGI-3's games are MIT; all are fetched, not vendored, and the instances in `data/` drawn from them keep their sources' licenses.

Continual-ARC is made by unify. unify is building continual learning for the agents companies have already built, training the model to drive their own harness, so the agent gets faster and cheaper the more it runs, on a model they own. We publish the research behind it. [...] - Nothing about ARC brought in. No ARC, Re-ARC, ARC-GEN or other task data, answers or solvers inside the learner, its prompts or its starting memory, and no rebuilding of the schedule. What a model learned in pretraining is its prior, which the learner's own reset on the same model already carries.

Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. # Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

unifyai

## Abstract

Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-AGI tasks, compares memory- and weight-based continual learning under frozen-weight agent harnesses, revealing that harness persistence rarely improves memorization and most harness methods underperform simple caching, while weight-based learning shows better generalization.

Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization.
